analysis.one_liner: Stops for-profit colleges from counting GI Bill and military tuition aid as private revenue.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 37 Senate cosponsors, the bill sat in committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law says for-profit colleges must get at least 10% of their revenue from sources other than federal student aid, or lose access to that aid. But GI Bill benefits and military tuition assistance currently count as that 'non-federal' 10%, so a for-profit school can collect nearly all its revenue from federal programs. This bill rewrites the rule so veterans' and service members' federal education benefits count as federal money, and it makes the Pentagon and Department of Veterans Affairs cut off schools that fail the test two years in a row [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Service members, veterans, and their families who use GI Bill and military tuition benefits. The change pressures for-profit colleges to compete for these students on quality rather than relying on them as guaranteed federal revenue, and it cuts off federal money to schools that depend almost entirely on government checks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Veterans and service members using education benefits

how_it_helps.text: Redefines the 90/10 rule so federal education benefits for military personnel and veterans (GI Bill chapters of title 38 and DoD tuition programs) count toward the federal-revenue limit instead of the 10% non-federal requirement [S2][S3].

Makes a for-profit college that misses the requirement two consecutive years ineligible for federal educational assistance — including Department of Defense and Department of Veterans Affairs programs — for at least two years, with a two-year path to regain eligibility [S3].
Requires the Secretaries of Defense and Veterans Affairs to notify affected service members and veterans and publish online the names of schools that lost eligibility, why, and for how long [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges that rely heavily on GI Bill and military tuition assistance for revenue. Some would have to shrink, raise private tuition, or recruit a broader mix of students; schools that fail the test lose access to all federal education funding for at least two years.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit colleges dependent on military and veterans' aid

drawbacks.text: Veterans enrolled at, or planning to attend, a school that loses eligibility would find that DoD and VA education benefits cannot be used there for the penalty period, which could disrupt some veterans' plans — including at schools some veterans choose for flexible or online programs [S3].

The bill strengthens the penalty from loss of federal student aid alone to disqualification from all federal education programs, and a school could rationally respond by capping how many veterans it enrolls rather than improving quality — an honest cost an supporter of the fix would acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but modest: veterans' benefits would no longer serve as a compliance loophole for for-profit colleges, in exchange for the possibility that some veterans lose access to specific schools or that schools cap veteran enrollment. Given that the same taxpayer dollars flow either way, the main gain is targeting — federal education money would stop propping up schools that live almost entirely on it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Carper introduced the bill on November 9, 2017, with 33 original Senate cosponsors named on the bill text [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
The cosponsor list grew to 37 — 35 Democrats and 2 independents — with no further action recorded [S4][S5].
The full action history shows only two entries: introduction and the committee referral, with no hearing, markup, or vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges that count GI Bill and military tuition assistance toward their required 10% non-federal revenue kept that revenue stream untouched. The bill never reached a vote, so the loophole remained open through the end of the 115th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges using veterans' aid as private revenue

for.name: Sen. Tom Carper
for.role: U.S. Senator from Delaware; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Military and Veterans Education Protection Act and recruited a broad Democratic cosponsor list.

for.name: 35 Senate Democrats and 2 Independent senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Durbin, Warren, Sanders, Tester, Duckworth, and King.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without a path to the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, with no Senate Republicans signing on, and the bill died in the Republican-chaired committee without a hearing or vote.

industries.note: The bill removes the biggest cushion in the 90/10 rule: GI Bill and military tuition dollars would no longer count as the school's 10% 'non-federal' revenue, so schools living on federal checks would have to change or lose eligibility. Their interest here runs against the service members and veterans whose benefits the schools rely on as guaranteed revenue.
For-profit colleges would face a tougher revenue test, tilting competition for veteran and military students toward schools that do not depend on federal aid for nearly all revenue.
